lesson.title: One Chain, One Shape: Folding Into Function
lesson.summary: Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of a single folded polypeptide, produced when the chemical properties of amino acid side chains pull distant parts of the chain together and lock it into a stable, functional form.
lesson.body:
Secondary structure describes local coils and sheets, but a working protein needs an overall three-dimensional shape, and that full folded shape of one polypeptide chain is called tertiary structure. Tertiary structure emerges as the side chains, the R groups introduced back in the amino acids concept, interact with one another and with the surrounding water, pulling together amino acids that might be dozens or even hundreds of positions apart in the primary sequence. The specific functional groups carried on each side chain, hydroxyls, amines, carboxylic acids, thiols, determine exactly which interactions are chemically possible, which is why tertiary folding is really an extension of side chain chemistry into three dimensions.

Several distinct types of interactions cooperate to hold a tertiary structure in place. Hydrophobic side chains tend to cluster together in the interior of the protein, away from the surrounding water, in what is called the hydrophobic effect, while polar and charged side chains generally remain on the exterior, in contact with water. Hydrogen bonds can form between polar side chains, and ionic bonds, sometimes called salt bridges, can form between oppositely charged side chains, such as the negatively charged carboxylate of aspartate pairing with the positively charged amine of lysine. In some proteins, two cysteine side chains, each carrying a sulfur containing thiol group, can be oxidized to form a covalent disulfide bond, a strong crosslink that adds extra stability, particularly in proteins that are secreted outside the cell.

This precise three-dimensional shape is not just structural decoration, it is what allows a protein to do its job. Myoglobin, the oxygen storage protein found in muscle tissue, folds into a compact globular tertiary structure that creates a snug hydrophobic pocket, and that pocket holds a nonprotein heme group whose iron atom binds a single molecule of oxygen. Change the fold even slightly and that pocket no longer fits the heme group correctly, and the protein loses its ability to bind oxygen at all.

Folding into the correct tertiary structure is not always automatic. Inside cells, a class of helper proteins called molecular chaperones, such as the GroEL and GroES complex found in many bacteria, assist newly made polypeptides in reaching their correct shape and prevent them from clumping together with other unfolded chains before folding is complete.

Tertiary structure is best understood as an assembly of smaller pieces rather than a shape built from scratch. The alpha helices and beta sheets described in secondary structure, along with the flexible loops and turns that connect them, are the actual building blocks that get packed together into the compact, three-dimensional arrangement of a finished tertiary structure. In proteins made of a single polypeptide chain, this is often the final level of structure, but in proteins built from more than one chain, folding continues one level further, into quaternary structure.
